rationale: A wins because it gives the founder four usable doors into coverage, not just three careful rooms with one missing wall. A's "When the software writes itself, you pay by the job - not by the seat" turns a small pricing fact into a real business-model story; B throws that lane away with "Pricing model analysis ... no_journalist_shape," which is too timid. B has discipline, but "AI Tools Have Crossed From Code Autocomplete to Full-Stack App Delivery" is the generic AI category lecture every launch thinks it deserves.
gaps_in_A: "while declining to publish a success rate" overstates the fact. The update says reliability is not disclosed, not that Replit actively declined.
"writes the code for students" jumps ahead of the evidence. The update says Replit is used heavily in education, but not that this agent is available to student accounts.
"the whole software industry is arguing about" is a sweepy trend claim without supplied evidence. The pricing angle is good, but that sentence needs outside proof or a smaller frame.
"newsjack-detector" as the next step is overcomplicated. The launch itself is the current peg; the immediate need is proof closure and reporter fit.
gaps_in_B: "Replit contradicting its own founding premise" is not in the update. Heavy education use is a fact; founding premise is decoration.
"the market has moved from AI that assists developers to AI that replaces the development workflow" turns one launch into a market shift. Even B admits it needs another comparable offering.

"Pricing model analysis ... no_journalist_shape" is a bad refusal. Usage-based pricing on top of subscriptions is a legitimate SaaS/business-model angle if rates, metering units, and customer cost examples can be obtained.
It leaves the human story on the table. The question "Can any named user ... be quoted" should have become a customer-story angle, not just a homework note.
